1.pericope_label: The widow's two mites; she of her penury cast in all the living she had

schools.summary: Set the scene before expounding it: the debate is over, the council has withdrawn, and the seated teacher watching the rich bring their gifts is taking a brief diversion from the strain of the preceding hours. Explain the word for treasury as a compound of the Persian term for a royal hoard with the Greek for guarding, and note it occurs in the New Testament only here, in the parallel and once in John. Then make the philological point that carries the story: the word chosen for the widow's poverty is not the usual one. It is built on working for one's living, occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and stands against the commoner term used in the parallel Gospel, which is the proper word for beggary. The distinction is worth drawing out -- she was needy and driven to work for a scanty maintenance, not a beggar. Note two smaller textual points: this Gospel writes truly where the parallel has Amen, and the better manuscripts drop the closing words about the offerings of God.

Begin with the furniture, since the hearers will not know it: a chest with an opening at the top, set near the altar on the right hand of those entering the house of God, into which the priests put whatever was given for the temple. Explain the name from its parts, the Persian word for riches and the Greek for keeping. Then draw the moral out of the watching itself, before any of the giving is described, and draw it in a single stroke: the same Lord who overthrew those who traded in his house also marks those who bring gifts to it, giving praise to the deserving and condemning the bad. That is the whole of the lesson, and it is better made briefly than at length.

Attend to the small realism of the scene. The treasury cannot have stood above him, since he was seated directly opposite it, which is why three of the versions omit the clause about looking up altogether. Then state the consolation plainly and without ornament, because it is the reason the story was preserved: the poor and the widow are regarded by him and are his care; their mean services, done in faith and from a principle of love, are not despised but are preferred before the greater services of others where faith and love are wanting. Note also that the word for those who gave out of their abundance carries the sense of what remained over, so that they gave much and still had a great deal left.

This is the place for the antiquarian detail, which is unusually rewarding here, but keep it in service of the point. The two coins together made the fourth part of the Roman penny; that quarter-piece was the smallest brass coin at Rome, but a smaller one circulated among the Jews, named from a verb meaning to fail. Then follow the English words back: our penny was once struck with a deep indented cross dividing it into four, so that broken in two it made the halfpenny and broken in four the fourthing, which we have corrupted into farthing; and mite comes either from the creature our ancestors took for the smallest of animals or from the Latin for a small thing, whence the French word for a crumb. Say that her being miserably poor is precisely what heightens the merit of the act.

Ask why the story is told twice, and give both answers. First, that charity to the poor is a main matter in religion, which our Lord took all occasions to commend. Second, and sharper: the scribes who devoured widows' houses had just been named, and it aggravates that charge if the poor widows were the best benefactors of the very funds those men administered. Then press the watching as warning and encouragement together. The eye that saw her sees whether we give largely and liberally in proportion to what we have or are sneaking and paltry in it, and goes further, to whether we give with a willing mind or grudgingly; men may satisfy themselves with excuses he knows to be frivolous. But it should also make us free of the desire that others know, for he sees in secret and will reward openly.

debates.question: What force has the word chosen for the widow's poverty?

sides.position: It is built on working for one's living and is kin to the word for hunger; it occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, where the parallel Gospel uses the proper word for beggary
It was carefully chosen to say that she, though needy and compelled to work for a scanty maintenance, was not a beggar as the commoner word suggested
It means miserably poor, and the depth of the poverty is precisely what heightens the merit of the act

outliers.note: Alone describes the furniture the story assumes -- a chest with an opening at the top set near the altar on the right hand of those entering, into which the priests put what was given for the temple -- and alone draws the moral out of the watching itself, that the same Lord who overthrew those who traded in his house also marks those who bring gifts to it, praising the deserving and condemning the rest.

Alone follows the English coin-words back to their origins, the penny once struck with a deep indented cross dividing it into four so that broken in two it made the halfpenny and broken in four the fourthing we have corrupted into farthing, and mite taken either from the creature our ancestors thought the smallest of animals or from the Latin for a small thing, whence the French word for a crumb.

Alone suggests a reason for the story standing where it does, that the scribes who devoured widows' houses had just been named, so that it aggravates the charge if the poor widows were the best benefactors of the very funds those men administered.
Alone fixes the hour: the debate was over and the council had withdrawn in defeat, and the watching of the rich at the treasury was a slight diversion from the strain of the preceding hours.

themes: And he looked up, and saw the rich men casting their gifts into the treasury
And he saw also a certain poor widow casting in thither two mites
For all these have of their abundance cast in unto the offerings of God: but she of her penury hath cast in all the living that she had

5.pericope_label: The goodly stones and gifts; there shall not be left one stone upon another

schools.summary: Give the hearers the building, because the admiration is unintelligible without it. Some of the substructure stones were enormous and the columns of the portico were single blocks of marble over forty feet high; the gifts were offerings hung on pillars and porches, of which the golden vine with which Herod adorned the columns is the standing example. Explain the older custom that lies behind such offerings, of hanging up in a temple the spoils and armour of the slain. Then take the word for those gifts and set it beside its near neighbour: the noun for a thing consecrated and the noun for a thing accursed come from one verb and differ only in the length of a vowel, so that the same root yields blessing in one form and cursing in the other. Note that the construction of the reply differs slightly from both parallels, and say the human thing -- that after the triumphal entry this must have come as a shock.

Identify the speakers carefully: these were the disciples, and though the parallel names only one there were evidently more, one perhaps opening the subject and the others joining him; and the question that follows was put later, on the Mount of Olives, not on the spot. Note that two of the versions turn the reply into a question -- are these the things you are gazing at with such delight? -- which sharpens it considerably. Keep the exposition close to the words and let the prophecy stand in its own plainness rather than softening it.

Be concrete about what the disciples were looking at, since the sources allow it. An eyewitness who measured the stones reports them forty-five cubits long, five high and six broad, brought from another country, and no engine then in use could have lifted or set them. The marble was so white that at a distance the building looked like a mountain of snow, and the gilding made it a splendid spectacle when the sun struck it. The gifts were hung on the walls and pillars by people delivered from imminent danger, in accomplishment of their vows. Then let the reply fall without commentary: it was literally fulfilled.

Take the exchange as a rebuke of misplaced admiration and generalise it at once, because that is where the passage bites. When we speak of the temple it should be of the presence of God in it, of the ordinances administered there, and of the communion his people have with him; it is a poor thing, when we speak of the church, to let our discourse dwell on its pomps and revenues and the dignities and powers of its officers, for the king's daughter is all glorious within. Note that the disciples expected their Master to be as affected by the sight as they were, and to regret its destruction as they did. Then give the reply its full weight, and bring out the double impossibility they must have felt: the building seemed too beautiful for anyone to pull down for pity, and too strong for anyone to be able to.

sides.position: Either the large squared blocks of the eastern wall or precious stones used in decorating the building itself
Stones of the substructure, some enormous, the columns of the portico being single blocks of marble over forty feet high
Blocks forty-five cubits long, five high and six broad, brought from another country, which no engine then in use could have lifted

outliers.note: Alone turns the disciples' admiration into a rule about how the church should be spoken of -- that when we speak of the temple it should be of the presence of God in it and the communion his people have with him there, and that it is a poor thing to let our discourse dwell on pomps and revenues and the dignities of officers, the king's daughter being all glorious within.

Alone reports measurements from a man who had lately measured the stones, and alone describes the effect of the building, marble so white that at a distance it looked like a mountain of snow and gilding that made it a splendid spectacle when the sun struck it.

Alone notices that two versions turn the reply into a question -- are these the things you are gazing at with such delight -- and alone observes that although the parallel names one speaker there were evidently more, and that the question which follows was put later on the Mount of Olives.

themes: And as some spake of the temple, how it was adorned with goodly stones and gifts, he said
As for these things which ye behold, the days will come, in the which there shall not be left one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down

8.pericope_label: Take heed that ye be not deceived; in your patience possess ye your souls

schools.summary: Note first that the word Christ in the impostor's claim is supplied by the translators; the sentence is better left in the vagueness of the Greek, where the bare "I am" had already become significant without a predicate. Then keep a tally of what is peculiar to this Gospel, because in this stretch it is nearly everything: the word for commotions occurs in no other, the verb for being terrified only here and at the end of this book, the pestilences and the phrase for fearful sights are its own, the clause marking persecution as preceding all the rest is its own, and the words about travail-pangs which the others have are absent. Point out the assonance of the nouns for famine and pestilence, which no English can carry over. Do not soften the plain denial that the end follows immediately, and note that the participle for being haled away was a technical term of Athenian law.

Answer the question the hearers will actually be asking, which is why such things are announced in advance at all. Because they disturb less when they come if they have been foreknown: darts strike the less which are foreseen. Then divide the two nouns, wars belonging to the enemy without and commotions to the citizen within, so that the hearer is warned he will be troubled from both quarters at once; and add that the last tribulation is preceded by many, so that many evils must come first before that evil which has no end. Finally read the ORDER of the calamities as itself the argument: first the hearts of men are disturbed and afterwards the elements, so that when the whole frame of things falls into confusion it may be plain from what retribution the ruin arises -- for these things spring not from injustice in the one who inflicts them but from the deserts of the world that suffers them.

Keep the identifications concrete: the wars are those of the Romans against that nation and the commotions its own internal seditions; the testimony is an opportunity of speaking for Christ before kings and rulers, which would confirm the speakers and stand as evidence against those before whom they were brought. On the closing sentence, note that the Latin, Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic all read it as a promise, ye shall possess. Then refuse the shallow comfort in the promise about the hair of the head. It cannot mean preservation from all bodily harm, since those addressed have just been told that some of them would be put to death; what is meant is that they should be no losers in the main, all things working together for their good, so that even death is to their advantage. And say the harder thing about defending life: Christ prescribes a defence contrary to what carnal reason dictates, that we be always exposed to death, and no man commits his soul to God rightly until he has learned to live each day prepared to die.

Mark that the words of the deceivers are quoted, not spoken -- it is they who say the time is near, not the speaker. Then be practical about the promised mouth and wisdom: a ready utterance joined to an irresistible eloquence, an abundance of wisdom to know what to say and the power to say it. On the hair of the head, take it as proverbial for suffering no essential injury, adding that nothing perishes without the special providence of God, and then not before the time nor without a full reward. On the closing command, prefer the manuscripts that read it as a promise -- ye shall preserve -- and take the sense inwardly as well as outwardly: be calm and serene, masters of yourselves and superior to all disquieting passions, since by keeping the government of your spirits you both avoid much misery and guard the better against every danger.

debates.question: What does "in your patience possess ye your souls" mean?

sides.position: By your endurance gain ye your lives; the verb involves acquiring rather than possessing, and the better manuscripts give it as a promise
Your perseverance will preserve your lives: ye shall escape the Roman sword and not perish in the destruction of the city
By persevering under trial you will save your lives, the word for souls meaning lives
Be calm and serene, masters of yourselves and superior to all disquieting passions
Possess that peace and joy which the world cannot take away; the versions read it as a promise, ye shall possess

Christ prescribes a defence of life contrary to what carnal reason dictates: we are to be always exposed to death, and no man commits his soul to God rightly until he has learned to live each day prepared to die

outliers.note: Alone explains why the troubles are announced in advance at all, that they disturb the less when they come if they have been foreknown, for darts strike the less which are foreseen; and alone reads the order of the calamities as itself the argument, that the hearts of men are disturbed first and the elements afterwards, so that when the frame of things falls into confusion it may be plain from what retribution the ruin arises.

Alone keeps a running tally of what is peculiar to this Gospel in this stretch -- the word for commotions, the verb for being terrified, the pestilences, the phrase for fearful sights, the clause putting persecution before all the rest -- and alone presses the promise of a mouth and wisdom into an argument against distinguishing an inspiration of thoughts from one of words, since men think through the medium of language.

Alone refuses to read the closing sentence as a promise of safety at all, holding that we are bidden to be always exposed to death and to walk through fire and water and sword, and that no man commits his soul to God rightly until he has learned to live from day to day constantly prepared to die.

Alone supplies a historical claim to match the promise about the hair of the head, that no Christian is thought to have perished in the calamities of the city because the community had withdrawn beforehand across the Jordan.

themes: Take heed that ye be not deceived: for many shall come in my name, saying, I am Christ; and the time draweth near
But before all these, they shall lay their hands on you, and persecute you
But there shall not an hair of your head perish. In your patience possess ye your souls

20.pericope_label: Jerusalem compassed with armies; trodden down till the times of the Gentiles

schools.summary: Put the weight on a tense, because the practical force of the warning depends on it: the participle for being encircled is a present, so the sign is the ring closing and not the siege completed -- it will be too late once the city is shut. Note that the Christians did in fact leave for Pella in time. Meet the objection that such words could not have been spoken before the armies came with the short answer that they could if predictive prophecy is possible at all. Treat this section as paraphrase rather than transcript: the days of vengeance answer to the great tribulation of the other reports, the reference to what has been written is peculiar to this Gospel, the word used for distress is not employed in that sense by the other evangelists, and the description of falling by the sword has nothing answering to it in the parallels. Give the numbers from the historian, about eleven hundred thousand dead and some ninety-seven thousand taken, while saying plainly that the figure is probably exaggerated though the true number must have been large. On the closing limit, note only that a limit to the punishment is implied, and that the same thought is developed at length in Romans.

Keep the identifications tight and do not speculate beyond them. The armies are the Roman force Titus brought, and three of the versions read the singular, one army, rather than several. The vengeance is God's vengeance on that nation for the rejection and crucifixion of the Messiah, and the things written are the threatenings of the prophets. That is as far as the text goes and as far as the exposition should.

Read the flight instruction as one connected piece of practical advice: those inside are to get out before the retreat is cut off by the converging forces, and those in the country are on no account to go in. Then give the aftermath, which is where this material is strongest. Eleven hundred thousand perished in the siege and above ninety thousand were sold for slaves; the land itself was sold by the emperor; no Jew was suffered even to come within sight of the city; the very foundations were ploughed up and a heathen temple built where the temple of God had stood. Then take the closing limit forward rather than backward: the times of the Gentiles are the times limited for their treading the city, and they terminate in the full conversion of the nations -- though when that shall be, we do not know.

Set this passage in its perspective before expounding the detail. Having given them an idea of the times for the next thirty-eight years, he now shows what all those things would issue in at last: the destruction of the city and the dispersion of the nation, which would be a little day of judgment and a type and figure of the second coming. Add the observation that makes the type intelligible -- that the destruction of Jerusalem would be as it were the destruction of the world to those whose hearts were bound up in it. Then take the sign in order: they should see the city besieged and compassed with armies, and seeing that, might conclude that its desolation was near, for in this the siege would infallibly end, though it might be long.

debates.question: What do the times of the Gentiles being fulfilled imply?

sides.position: A restoration: the punishment of Israel and the desolation of the city were to have a limit, a thought developed at length in Romans, where the fulness of the Gentiles is a distinct echo of this phrase
Only that the punishment has a limit; what more it means is not clear
That the nations given dominion over the land will have accomplished what the Lord appointed them, and that their conversion will then take place -- but when, we do not know
The times limited for their treading the city, terminating in the full conversion of the Gentiles
Doubtful whether restoration is in view here at all; there is no great reason to think those times will be fulfilled before the end of the world itself

outliers.note: Alone rests the practical force of the warning on a tense, that the participle for being encircled is a present so the sign is the ring closing and not the siege completed; and alone answers the objection that such words could not have been spoken before the armies came, replying that they could if predictive prophecy is possible at all.

Alone doubts that the restoration of the city is in view in this verse, says he can see no great reason to affirm that the times of the Gentiles will be fulfilled before the end of the world itself, and declines to press his own conjecture; he adds that he cannot but wonder the disciples, having heard this so plainly, should so soon be asking whether the kingdom would at that time be restored to Israel.

Alone carries the treading down forward through later history, arguing that the bondage has been long and oppressive as the city passed from Roman to Saracen to Turkish hands, and reaching for the ancient image of a conqueror setting his foot on the neck of the captive.
Alone states why the fall of the city can serve as a figure of the last judgment, that it would be as it were the destruction of the world to those whose hearts were bound up in it.

themes: And when ye shall see Jerusalem compassed with armies, then know that the desolation thereof is nigh
For these be the days of vengeance, that all things which are written may be fulfilled
And Jerusalem shall be trodden down of the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles be fulfilled

25.pericope_label: Signs in the sun and moon; look up, for your redemption draweth nigh

schools.summary: Work through the vocabulary of terror, which is unusually rich here: the noun for distress means anguish, the phrase for perplexity describes a man who has lost his road, the word for the roaring is the one that gives us echo, and the word for the waves is an old term for the swell of the sea. Note that the verb for hearts failing means literally to breathe out the soul, that it is used by this evangelist alone, and that it is the sort of word which would come naturally to a physician. Then take a position on the coming and say which you take. If you refer it to the second advent, note that the wording is deliberately unhurried -- it will be not till then, and the time element is left purposely vague. If you refer it to the fall of the city, then the redemption drawing near is the end of Jewish power and the deliverance of the disciples from persecution in that country, which is what the word for redemption points to in its primary sense here.

Two things are worth doing here that nobody else will do. First, meet the objection that the prophecy is fulfilled already by the troubles of the present age. Answer that it is not, since the evils now suffered fall alike on the good and the bad and are common to both kingdoms, whereas the tribulation meant will belong to the Church troubled by the world rather than to those who trouble it -- for they are the ones who shall say, Peace and safety. Second, read the coming itself as one in which he comes now, in his members as in clouds, or in the Church as in one great cloud. Then turn to consolation, since the discourse does: having spoken against the reprobate it now comforts the elect. Read the gesture inwardly -- in scripture the head often stands for the mind, since as the members are ruled by the head so the thoughts are governed by the mind, and to lift the head is to raise the mind toward the joys of the country above. When the buffetings of the world multiply, rejoice: when the world whose friend you are not draws to its close, the redemption you seek is near.

State why the consolation is placed just here, since the structure is the argument: the joy of the godly had to be set against the general sorrow and distress of the world, and the difference between them and the reprobate pointed out, so that they should not view the coming of Christ with horror. Add the general principle it rests on -- that scripture describes the same judgments, and not only the last, quite differently according to whether it addresses believers or unbelievers, so that the day of the Lord is darkness and gloominess to the one and light to the other. Keep the exposition of the signs brief: the sun and moon darkened and suffering strange eclipses, and the hearts of men failing for fear of what those signs portend.

Distinguish these signs from those mentioned earlier in the chapter, and say that the great day is what is in view, of which the destruction of the city was the type. Take the roaring sea as a figure for the Roman armies that were to overrun the country, and prefer the rendering of the following phrase as coming upon this land rather than upon the earth. Then keep the closing command simple and warm: look up with firm faith and lift up your heads with joy, for the redemption out of many troubles draws near.

debates.question: What coming is meant, and when?

sides.position: The second advent, and the wording is deliberately unhurried -- it will be not till then, and the time element is left purposely vague
The judgment on the city: the redemption drawing near means the end of Jewish power, when the disciples would be completely delivered from persecution in that country
Primarily the deliverance which followed the destruction of the city, when the Church was freed from what had been its most formidable danger
Not the evils of the present age, which fall alike on good and bad; the coming meant is that whereby he comes now in his members as in clouds, or in the Church as in one great cloud
The great day, of which the destruction of the city was the type; the signs here differ from those named earlier

outliers.note: Alone meets the objection that the prophecy is already fulfilled by the troubles of the present age, answering that those evils fall alike on the good and the bad and are common to both kingdoms, whereas the tribulation meant will belong to the Church troubled by the world and not to those who trouble it, since it is they who shall say Peace and safety.

Alone reads the lifting of the head inwardly, on the ground that in scripture the head often stands for the mind, as the members are ruled by the head so the thoughts are governed by the mind, so that to lift the head is to raise the mind toward the joys of the country above.

Alone observes that the verb for hearts failing is used by this evangelist only, that it means literally to breathe out the soul, and that it is the sort of word which would enter naturally into the vocabulary of a physician.
Alone takes the roaring sea as a figure for the Roman armies by which the country was to be overrun and destroyed.

themes: And there shall be signs in the sun, and in the moon, and in the stars; and upon the earth distress of nations, with perplexity
And then shall they see the Son of man coming in a cloud with power and great glory
And when these things begin to come to pass, then look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh

29.pericope_label: The fig tree and all the trees; heaven and earth shall pass away

schools.summary: Begin with what this Gospel adds: where the others keep to the fig tree alone, this one says all the trees. That is true of them all, though the fig was the commonest in the country, and it marks the occasion -- the words were spoken just before the Passover, when the spring was visible in every grove, and were probably suggested by what the disciples could see from the hill where they sat. Note the vocabulary lightly: the verb for shooting forth occurs only here and once in Acts, and the season named is summer, not harvest. Then handle the saying about this generation honestly, because it is the hardest sentence in the chapter and gives critics a great deal of trouble. Lay the positions out. Some apply the words to the whole discourse together, and of those some conclude the speaker was mistaken and others that he was not accurately reported; others confine them to the destruction of the city, which did happen within that generation. Grant the force of the second, since it is not easy in so long a discourse to tell where one subject ends and the other begins, and pass on the solution that the destruction of the city is meant, but regarded as the type of the end of the world.

Keep this brief and exact. The parable is spoken to the disciples; the shooting forth is of buds, branches and leaves, and one version adds that they do it of themselves; the things to be seen are the signs already given. Note that the Oriental versions read all these things in the promise, agreeing with the parallel. Where the text refers the reader elsewhere, refer him, and do not manufacture material the verse does not carry.

Say what season it was, since the parable depends on it: spring, just before the Passover, with all the trees budding on the mount where they then were. Make something of the phrase about knowing it of yourselves -- that none need teach it. Then take the kingdom's nearness as the displacement of the old order by the new: after the destruction of the Jewish state the doctrine of Christ crucified would be preached everywhere and everywhere prevail, the fall of city, temple and religion making way for the advancement of that kingdom. On the disputed saying, take the narrower reading and say so plainly, referring all things to what had been spoken of the destruction of Jerusalem, which is what the disciples' original question asked about; and gloss the phrase as this race of men.

Use the parable as it is meant, as an instruction in reading providence. As in the kingdom of nature there is a chain of causes, so in the kingdom of providence one event follows upon another; and as we may lawfully expect the change of the seasons once the second causes have begun to work, so we may expect something uncommon when God is already raised up out of his holy habitation. Give the two applications the comparison yields. When we see a nation filling up the measure of its iniquity we may conclude that its ruin is near; and when we see the ruin of persecuting powers hastening on, we may infer that the kingdom of God is at hand, since it gains ground once the opposition to it is removed.

debates.question: What does "this generation shall not pass away" cover?

sides.position: The question gives critics great trouble; some apply it to the whole discourse and conclude either that the speaker was mistaken or that he was misreported, others confine it to the destruction of the city, which did happen within that generation. The best solution offered is that the destruction is meant, but regarded as the type of the end of the world
All that had been spoken of the destruction of Jerusalem, to which the disciples' original question related
This race of men
The Oriental versions read "all these things" here, agreeing with the parallel

debates.question: In what sense is the kingdom of God nigh?

sides.position: The consummation of the kingdom is meant, not its beginning
After the destruction of the Jewish state the doctrine of Christ crucified would be preached everywhere and everywhere prevail
The destruction of the Jewish city, temple and religion, to make way for the advancement of that kingdom
When the opposition given to it is removed it shall gain ground; the ruin of persecuting powers is the sign

outliers.note: Alone lays out the whole controversy over "this generation" without adopting a side, reporting that some apply the words to the entire discourse and conclude either that the speaker was mistaken or that he was misreported, that others confine them to the destruction of the city, and that the best solution offered is that the destruction is meant but regarded as the type of the end of the world.

Alone takes the addition of all the trees as evidence of the occasion, the words having been spoken just before the Passover when the spring was visible in every grove, and probably suggested by what the disciples could see from the hill where they sat; he recalls that one such tree had lately been found in full foliage.

Alone turns the parable into an instruction in reading providence, that as in nature there is a chain of causes so in providence one event follows on another, so that a nation filling up the measure of its iniquity may be known to be near its ruin.

themes: Behold the fig tree, and all the trees; when they now shoot forth, ye see and know of your own selves that summer is now nigh at hand
Verily I say unto you, This generation shall not pass away, till all be fulfilled
Heaven and earth shall pass away: but my words shall not pass away

34.pericope_label: Lest your hearts be overcharged; watch ye therefore and pray always

schools.summary: Note that the word for surfeiting belonged more or less to medical vocabulary and means the nausea that follows a debauch, and that this closing warning is another stretch with nothing answering to it in the parallel reports. List what is peculiar in it: this evangelist alone uses the words for overcharged and for surfeiting, and he and Paul alone those for drunkenness, for the cares of this life and for unawares -- and observe that the passage falls in with a tendency of this Gospel to record whatever warned men against sensuality and worldliness. Explain the snare from fowling, a net sprung quickly on birds that are not expecting it. Take the command to watch as the pith of the whole discourse, deriving the verb from being sleepless, and the aim as standing before the Son of man without dread. On the closing verses, note that the word for lodging meant strictly to pass the night not in a room but in a courtyard, and was used in military language for a bivouac -- which suits the accounts that most of those nights were spent in a garden.

Read the two dangers against the parallel warning about flight, and read them allegorically: the cares of this life answer to its winter, mournful as winter is, and the surfeiting and drunkenness to its sabbath, since a day given over to worldly pleasure buries the heart in luxury while the spiritual sabbath is lost. Then make the example the point, which is where this material is strongest. The one who bid us watch and pray before the coming of the Judge and the uncertain end of each of us was himself, as the time of his Passion drew near, instant in teaching, watching and prayer -- confirming by his own example what he had commanded in word, and showing that it is a thing worthy of God both to watch and by word and deed to point out the way of truth to a neighbour.

Explain why the people heard him gladly, since the closing verse turns on it: his speech was with power, and with authority he applied to spiritual worship the things which had been delivered in figures by Moses and the prophets. Then take the detail of the hour and make it prayer rather than chronology. Those who came to him before light might with fitness say the words of the psalm, O God my God, early do I wait upon you.

Ask the question the warning raises and do not dodge it: was there need to warn the apostles themselves against gluttony and drunkenness? If there was, then there is reason to warn even strong Christians against the grossest sins, and no one is wise who thinks himself out of the reach of any sin. Keep the physical sense of the word -- to be made heavy, as those are who have eaten or drunk too much -- and turn it into the counsel that we not be rendered secure by an improper use of lawful things, nor make this earth our portion. Attach the word for continually to the watching as well as the praying, since no man is safe at any time who does not take that advice as literally as possible. Then close on the rising, and press it: he did not waste his mornings in idleness or sleep, and his hearers were happier at those early lectures than the slumbers of the morning could have made them.

Keep this one short and turn it inward. Taking heed to yourselves means to your souls and bodies, your lives and conversations: be upon your watch and guard. That is the whole of what the verse asks, and the exposition does not need to be longer than the command.

debates.question: What is the scope of the warning and the snare?

sides.position: The face of this whole land, that is Judea, on which these judgments were to fall
Judea: as birds are caught by a net sprung on them suddenly, so shall these troubles come upon that land
The day of judgment or of death, coming unawares even on those who are not of this world
The word for snare is absent from the other Gospels though Paul uses it several times; the whole passage answers to this Gospel's care to record warnings against sensuality and worldliness

outliers.note: Alone reads the two dangers against the parallel warning about flight in winter or on the sabbath, taking the cares of this life to answer to the winter, mournful as winter is, and the surfeiting and drunkenness to answer to the sabbath, since a day given to worldly pleasure buries the heart in luxury while the spiritual sabbath is lost.

Alone makes the closing verses an argument from example rather than a note of itinerary, observing that the one who bid us watch and pray before the coming of the Judge was himself, as his Passion drew near, instant in teaching, watching and prayer, and so confirmed by his own conduct what he had commanded in word.

Alone explains why the people heard him gladly, that his speech was with power and that he applied to spiritual worship what had been delivered in figures by Moses and the prophets; and alone turns the detail of the early hour into prayer, that those who came before light might fitly say the psalm's words, early do I wait upon you.

Alone explains that the word for lodging meant strictly to pass the night not in a room but in a courtyard, and was used in military language for a bivouac, which suits the accounts that most of those nights were spent in a garden rather than a house.

Alone presses the early rising into a rule of life, that his hearers were happier at those early lectures than the slumbers of the morning could have made them, and that we should not scruple to deny ourselves unnecessary sleep in order to place ourselves morning after morning at his feet.

themes: And take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life
Watch ye therefore, and pray always, that ye may be accounted worthy to escape all these things
And in the day time he was teaching in the temple; and at night he went out, and abode in the mount that is called the mount of Olives
